entries.answer_gold: Assuming Andres meets the stated condition, they may cast one or both exiled cards.

entries.question: Aminah has no cards in their library and activate [Words of Wind] in their upkeep. Do they lose the game?
entries.reason: Both conclude Words of Wind's replacement effect prevents the draw from being attempted (so Aminah does not lose).
entries.answer:
No — activating Words of Wind does not make Aminah lose, and in fact it protects them from the next draw they would make this turn.

Words of Wind reads: "{1}: The next time you would draw a card this turn, each player returns a permanent they control to its owner's hand instead." That's a replacement effect on the draw itself. Merely activating it in the upkeep step doesn't draw anything, so nothing happens involving the empty library at that time; the effect just waits in place.

Then, in Aminah's draw step, the turn-based draw would happen — but Words of Wind replaces it, so no card is ever drawn from the empty library. Instead, each player (Aminah and each opponent) returns a permanent they control to its owner's hand. Because the draw is replaced rather than attempted, Aminah never tries to draw from an empty library and so isn't put in the position that would cost them the game.

Notes and caveats:
- This works for any number of players: the returning effect hits each player who controls a permanent, so at a multiplayer table every player, not just one opponent, returns one.
- If Aminah activates Words of Wind more than once, they can choose which instance to apply and use up each time they would draw a card ([Words of Wind ruling #0]) — one instance per draw, so multiple draws in a turn need multiple activations.
- The protection lasts only for that turn ("this turn"). On a later turn with an empty library and no replacement effect in place, Aminah would have to attempt the draw again.
- The specific numbered rule stating that a player attempting to draw from an empty library loses the game was not included in the context provided to me, so I'm relying on Words of Wind's own text that the draw is replaced and therefore never attempted.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: No. Even though there are no there are no cards in Aminah's library and therefore no cards could be drawn, Words of Wind's replacement effect will still apply and replace the draw as normal.

entries.question: Allan controls [Living Inferno]. They activate it, targeting Nathaly's [Runeclaw Bear]. In response, Nathaly casts [Chemister's Trick], targeting the Living Inferno. How much damage will be dealt to Runeclaw Bear when the Living Inferno's ability resolves?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude that Living Inferno's damage division is locked in when the ability is activated, so the Bear takes the 8 damage Allan allocated despite Chemister's Trick resolving first.
entries.answer:
Runeclaw Bear will be dealt 8 damage — the full amount locked in when Allan activated Living Inferno's ability, unaffected by Chemister's Trick's -2/-0.

Why: because Living Inferno's ability divides damage among targets, the amount of damage it will deal is locked in as the ability is activated, based on Living Inferno's power at that time (8). Later changes to Living Inferno's power — such as the -2/-0 from Nathaly's Chemister's Trick resolving first — don't change that number [Living Inferno ruling #0][Living Inferno ruling #1].

Since Runeclaw Bear was the only target, all 8 damage goes to it, which is lethal to a 2/2. In return, when Living Inferno's ability resolves, Runeclaw Bear deals damage equal to its power to Living Inferno; that amount is determined on resolution, not on activation [Living Inferno ruling #1], so Runeclaw Bear deals 2 damage to Living Inferno. Living Inferno is a 6/5 at that moment due to Chemister's Trick, so 2 damage isn't lethal to it.

Note that Chemister's Trick also makes Living Inferno "attack this turn if able," but Living Inferno was tapped to pay the {T} in its ability's cost, so it won't attack [Chemister's Trick ruling #0]. Nothing here depends on the number of players, so the answer is the same in a two-player or multiplayer game.

Timing assumption: Chemister's Trick was cast in response and so resolves before Living Inferno's ability. If instead the -2/-0 had somehow applied before the ability was activated, Living Inferno would have been a 6/5 at activation and would only have locked in 6 damage.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: 8. Since Living Inferno divides its damage among multiple targets, Allan announces the division while activating the ability. It won't change later, even if Living Inferno's power changes.

entries.question: After both players finish taking mulligans, Adrian is going second and has both [Gemstone Caverns] and [Chancellor of the Annex] in their hand. Can they reveal Chancellor of the Annex for its ability and also exile it to begin the game with Gemstone Caverns on the battlefield?
entries.reason: Both answers reach the same final ruling: Adrian may reveal Chancellor of the Annex from their opening hand and then exile it to put Gemstone Caverns onto the battlefield (order matters, reveal first).
entries.answer:
Yes. Adrian may reveal Chancellor of the Annex from their opening hand and then exile that same Chancellor of the Annex as the cost for putting Gemstone Caverns onto the battlefield.

Why: Both cards grant actions taken from the opening hand (the hand after all mulligans are complete). The starting player takes all of their opening-hand actions first, in any order, then each other player in turn order [Gemstone Caverns ruling #0] [Chancellor of the Annex ruling #2]. Since Adrian is going second, Adrian takes their actions after the starting player, and Adrian chooses the order of their own actions. So Adrian first reveals Chancellor of the Annex, which sets up its effect ("when each opponent casts their first spell of the game, counter that spell unless that player pays {1}"). That revealed effect is established by the act of revealing from the opening hand; it does not require Chancellor of the Annex to stay in hand afterward. Adrian then begins the game with Gemstone Caverns on the battlefield with a luck counter, exiling Chancellor of the Annex as the required "exile a card from your hand."

If Adrian did it in the opposite order — exiling Chancellor of the Annex first — the card would already be in the exile zone and no longer in the opening hand, so it could not then be revealed from hand for its ability. Order matters here, so reveal first.

Multiplayer note: the same works with more than two players; the revealed Chancellor of the Annex effect triggers each time an opponent casts their first spell of the game, i.e., once per opponent [Chancellor of the Annex ruling #1]. In a two-player game it simply applies to the one opponent. Note also the tax is {1} generic mana (payable with any color or colorless), not {C}.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Yes. Adrian can choose to use these two card's effects in either order. Therefore they could use Chancellor of the Annex's effect first and then use Gemstone Caverns's.

entries.question: Aspen controls [Cosima, God of the Voyage] and mutates [Snapdax, Apex of the Hunt] onto it, putting it underneath Cosima, God of the Voyage. At the beginning of their next upkeep, Aspen exiles Cosima, God of the Voyage to its own triggered ability. What happens?
entries.reason: The candidate says only Cosima's ability functions and Snapdax provides nothing, while the reference states both cards are exiled and both grant triggered abilities (so you get both triggers referring to Cosima in exile).
entries.answer:
Direct answer: Aspen may exile the mutated permanent, and doing so puts both physical cards — Cosima, God of the Voyage and Snapdax, Apex of the Hunt — into exile as two separate cards; the mutated permanent no longer exists. Only Cosima, God of the Voyage carries the granted ability ("Whenever a land you control enters, if Cosima is exiled, you may put a voyage counter on it. If you don't, return Cosima to the battlefield with X +1/+1 counters on it and draw X cards"), so only Cosima, God of the Voyage can come back later, and it comes back as a plain 2/4 Cosima, God of the Voyage — a brand-new object with none of Snapdax, Apex of the Hunt's abilities (no double strike, no mutate trigger). Snapdax, Apex of the Hunt simply stays in exile.

Details and assumptions:
- Cosima, God of the Voyage's ability triggers only if it is on the battlefield at the beginning of Aspen's upkeep, and Aspen may exile it only if it is still on the battlefield as that ability resolves [Cosima, God of the Voyage // The Omenkeel ruling #13]. Here the mutated permanent is Cosima, God of the Voyage (it's the top card), so that works.
- Each land entering under Aspen's control afterward triggers the granted ability; on resolution the game checks that Cosima, God of the Voyage is still in exile, and if it has left exile the ability does nothing [Cosima, God of the Voyage // The Omenkeel ruling #11]. Aspen may choose to return it even with zero voyage counters, drawing no cards and getting no +1/+1 counters [Cosima, God of the Voyage // The Omenkeel ruling #5]. Players cannot respond to the counter-or-return choice [Cosima, God of the Voyage // The Omenkeel ruling #8].
- Because the returned Cosima, God of the Voyage is a new object (a card that left a zone and came back is a new object, per the principle cited in [603.7c]), it is not still mutated and does not gain Snapdax, Apex of the Hunt's abilities. Snapdax, Apex of the Hunt's "Whenever this creature mutates" trigger does not fire again, and nothing returns it.
- Caveat on grounding: the numbered mutate rules were not provided in my context. The closest provided analogue is the merged-permanent rule for meld, [712.21c], which states that when a melded permanent leaves the battlefield one permanent leaves and both cards go to the appropriate zone — the same principle I'm applying to the mutated pile here. If your table wants the literal mutate rule text, look it up; the outcome above matches standard mutate behavior.
- Player count: nothing here depends on the number of opponents, so the answer is the same in a two-player game and at a multiplayer table. (One multiplayer wrinkle from the provided rules: if the controller of a delayed return ability leaves the game, the ability isn't put on the stack and the card never returns [800.4d] — but here Aspen controls both the exile and the return.)

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold:
Cosima, God of the Voyage and Snapdax, Apex of the Hunt both get exiled and gain the corresponding triggered ability. 

The ability on Snapdax, Apex of the Hunt still refers to Cosima, God of the Voyage in exile, so whenever a land enters the battlefield under Aspen's control, they can choose to put up to 2 counters on Cosima, God of the Voyage, and if they chooses not to for both triggers, they'll draw twice that many cards.

entries.question: Aubrey controls [Whiskervale Forerunner] and casts [Growth Cycle] to give it +3/+3. Before it resolves, Aubrey casts [Cooperate] choosing to copy Growth Cycle and changes the target to another creature. Does Whiskervale Forerunner trigger again?
entries.reason: Both the candidate and reference conclude Whiskervale Forerunner does not trigger again (the copy doesn't target it after Cooperate's target changes), so they reach the same final ruling.
entries.answer:
No. Whiskervale Forerunner does not trigger a second time.

Two independent reasons:

1. The copy of Growth Cycle created by Cooperate doesn't target Whiskervale Forerunner at all — Aubrey changed the copy's target to another creature, which Cooperate expressly permits ("You may choose new targets for the copy") [Refuse // Cooperate ruling #18]. Whiskervale Forerunner's valiant ability only triggers when Whiskervale Forerunner itself becomes the target of a spell or ability Aubrey controls.

2. Even if the copy had kept Whiskervale Forerunner as its target, valiant triggers only "for the first time each turn." Casting Growth Cycle at Whiskervale Forerunner already used up that trigger this turn. A copy on the stack can trigger valiant, but only if the creature hasn't already been targeted by a spell or ability you control this turn [Refuse // Cooperate ruling #1].

Timing/order note: I'm assuming Growth Cycle was cast targeting Whiskervale Forerunner first (triggering valiant then), then Cooperate copied it. The valiant trigger from Growth Cycle resolves before Growth Cycle itself [Whiskervale Forerunner ruling #2], and the Growth Cycle copy resolves before the original Growth Cycle [Refuse // Cooperate ruling #14]. If instead the copy had been the thing that first targeted Whiskervale Forerunner this turn (i.e., original Growth Cycle targeted something else and the copy was pointed at Whiskervale Forerunner), valiant would trigger off the copy [Refuse // Cooperate ruling #1].

Also relevant to the copy's size: Growth Cycle's bonus is locked in as it begins to resolve, and Growth Cycle isn't in the graveyard while it's still on the stack, so it doesn't count itself [Growth Cycle ruling #0][Growth Cycle ruling #1].

None of this depends on player count — the answer is the same in a two-player game or at a multiplayer table.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: No. When copying spells that allow the copies controller to change the target, the targets are changed before the spell is put onto the stack. There is never a point in time where the spell is targeting Whiskervale Forerunner before the targets are changed.

entries.question: Nico has a [Pillarfield Ox] and a [Skullbriar, the Walking Grave] with 3 +1/+1 counters in their graveyard. Arjun casts [Ghastly Conscription], targeting Nico. What happens to the counters on the Skullbriar, the Walking Grave? Will Nico know which manifested card is which?
entries.reason: The candidate asserts the +1/+1 counters remain on Skullbriar on the battlefield, whereas the reference states the counters cease to exist when it becomes a face-down permanent (though their prior existence lets Nico identify it).
entries.answer:
The three +1/+1 counters stay with Skullbriar, the Walking Grave, and yes — that will effectively tell everyone which manifested permanent is Skullbriar, the Walking Grave, because it will be a face-down 2/2 with three +1/+1 counters on it (a 5/5), while the manifested Pillarfield Ox will be a plain face-down 2/2.

Why the counters survive: Skullbriar, the Walking Grave's own text says "Counters remain on Skullbriar as it moves to any zone other than a player's hand or library." Ghastly Conscription moves it graveyard → exile → battlefield, and neither of those is a hand or library, so the counters persist through both moves. This card text overrides the general expectation that counters cease to exist when a permanent card changes zones. Per Skullbriar, the Walking Grave ruling #5, it retains all counters, not just +1/+1 counters, and per ruling #2 counters affecting power/toughness apply even in non-battlefield zones (so it's a 4/4 card while in the face-down exile pile).

An important consequence: once it's manifested, the face-down permanent has no name, no mana cost, no creature types, and no abilities (Ghastly Conscription ruling #8) — so it no longer has the counter-retention ability while face down. Compare Skullbriar, the Walking Grave ruling #1: the ability only works if the object has it in the zone it's leaving. So if that face-down permanent later leaves the battlefield while still face down, the counters will cease to exist. Turn it face up (a special action, revealing it and paying {B}{G}, per Ghastly Conscription ruling #2 and #5's framework) and it has the ability again.

Who controls and who knows what: Arjun cast Ghastly Conscription, so Arjun manifests and controls both face-down permanents; Nico only owns the cards. Nico may not look at face-down permanents Nico doesn't control (Ghastly Conscription ruling #13), and the pile is shuffled precisely to hide the identities (ruling #3). But the visible +1/+1 counters defeat that concealment here: the counters are public information on the battlefield, so Nico (and everyone) can identify the counter-laden face-down creature as Skullbriar, the Walking Grave and the other as Pillarfield Ox. Also note Ghastly Conscription ruling #9 — the players must keep clear which face-down permanent is which and how each became face down.

Assumption on timing: I'm treating the counters as already on Skullbriar, the Walking Grave in the graveyard before Ghastly Conscription resolves, as stated. If instead the counters were somehow removed before resolution, the manifested card would just be a face-down 2/2 and would be indistinguishable from the manifested Pillarfield Ox.

Multiplayer: Ghastly Conscription targets a single player, so nothing changes with more than two players — only Nico's graveyard is affected, and Arjun still controls all the manifested permanents; the counters are public info to every player at the table.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: When in the graveyard, Skullbriar, the Walking Grave had the ability that allowed it to keep its counters, so it is exiled and shuffled with 3 +1/+1 counters. When it's moved to the battlefield, it's face down and no longer has that ability, so the counters cease to exist. It had the counters immediately before entering the battlefield however, so Nico will know which face-down permanent is the Skullbriar, the Walking Grave and which is the Pillarfield Ox.

entries.question: Avery activates [Ascendant Spirit]'s first ability. Before it resolves Avery casts [Slip Out the Back] targeting Ascendant Spirit. When it phases back in, what will it look like?
entries.reason: Both say it will phase in as a 2/2 (not a Warrior) because the activated ability resolved while it was phased out and therefore did nothing.
entries.answer:
Ascendant Spirit phases back in as its normal self — a 1/1 blue Snow Creature — Spirit — with the +1/+1 counter Slip Out the Back put on it, so it's a 2/2 Spirit. It will NOT be a 2/3 Spirit Warrior, because the first ability did nothing.

Why: I'm assuming the ordering you described — the first ability of Ascendant Spirit was activated first, then Slip Out the Back was cast on top of it, so Slip Out the Back resolves first. Slip Out the Back puts a +1/+1 counter on Ascendant Spirit and phases it out. "Phases out" means the permanent (and anything attached to it) is treated as though it doesn't exist until its controller's next turn [Slip Out the Back]. A phased-out permanent can't be affected by spells or abilities and is treated as nonexistent [Slip Out the Back ruling #1], so when the activated ability of Ascendant Spirit then resolves, there is no Ascendant Spirit on the battlefield for it to make into a Spirit Warrior with base power and toughness 2/3; the ability simply does nothing. None of Ascendant Spirit's abilities has a duration, but an ability that never applied leaves nothing behind [Ascendant Spirit ruling #8].

Ascendant Spirit phases in during Avery's untap step, immediately before Avery untaps their permanents, and it keeps the counters it had when it phased out — so the +1/+1 counter is still there, making it 2/2 [Slip Out the Back ruling #2]. Phasing in doesn't trigger enters-the-battlefield abilities [Slip Out the Back ruling #3], and it can attack or pay {T} costs that turn [Slip Out the Back ruling #2]. Avery can, of course, activate the first ability again ({S}{S}) after it phases in to make it a 2/3 Spirit Warrior [Ascendant Spirit ruling #9].

If instead the ability had resolved before Slip Out the Back (i.e., Slip Out the Back was cast after the ability finished resolving), Ascendant Spirit would already be a Spirit Warrior with base power and toughness 2/3, and it would phase back in that way — 3/4 with the +1/+1 counter — since that ability has no duration [Ascendant Spirit ruling #8], [Ascendant Spirit ruling #4].

This interaction doesn't depend on player count; it works the same in a two-player game or at a multiplayer table.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: It will be a 2/2 and not a Warrior. When Ascendant Spirit's ability resolves it's phased out and won't be affected.

entries.question: Aspen controls [Parallel Lives] and a [Caldera Hellion]. They cast [Rite of Replication] targeting the Caldera Hellion. Can Aspen apply the devour replacement effect before the Parallel Lives replacement effect, sacrificing 1 creature to have each token enter with a +1/+1 counter?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude Parallel Lives must be applied before Caldera Hellion's devour and that a single sacrificed creature can only be used once, so it can add a +1/+1 counter to only one token.
entries.answer:
No. Aspen must apply Parallel Lives' replacement effect first, and even then a single sacrificed creature can only give a +1/+1 counter to one of the tokens, not all of them.

Why Parallel Lives goes first: a token entering the battlefield is an event contained within the event of creating that token. When one replacement effect applies to an event and another applies to an event contained within it, the outer one must be chosen first — so the token-doubling of Parallel Lives is applied before any "as this enters" effects such as devour on the resulting tokens [616.1g]. Devour is not an ordering option here at all; it's a replacement effect modifying how each token enters, and it can't be applied to a token that doesn't exist yet.

So, unkicked Rite of Replication creates 1 token, doubled by Parallel Lives to 2 tokens that are copies of Caldera Hellion (kicked, 5 becomes 10) [Parallel Lives ruling #0]. Each token has Devour 1 and each devour works as the token enters [Rite of Replication ruling #11].

Why one sacrifice doesn't feed them all: when multiple permanents with devour are entering at the same time, you may use each one's devour, but the same object can't be chosen to be sacrificed more than once across those replacement effects [614.13b] [Caldera Hellion ruling #3]. Sacrificing 1 creature therefore puts one +1/+1 counter on exactly one token; the others enter with zero counters. Note also that the tokens can't devour each other or themselves [Caldera Hellion ruling #1].

One practical warning: each Caldera Hellion token's triggered ability deals 3 damage to each creature, and tokens that devoured nothing are 3/3s, so that damage will be lethal to them [Caldera Hellion ruling #4].

This analysis doesn't depend on the number of players; Parallel Lives and the devour choices are all made by Aspen as the affected permanents' controller, so it's identical at a two-player or multiplayer table (APNAP ordering in [616.1g] only matters when different players choose simultaneously).

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: No. There are two replacement effects trying to apply to the original event of creating a Caldera Hellion: Caldera Hellion's own effect and Parallel Lives's effect. Caldera Hellion's effect applies to it entering the battlefield however, while Parallel Lives's effect applies to it being created, so Parallel Lives's effect must be applied first. After that is applied the original Caldera Hellion's effect doesn't exist anymore, but each of the new Caldera Hellions entering the battlefield has its own effect, which can now be applied individually.

entries.question: Aubrey controls [Exotic Orchard]. Nikolas controls [Crumbling Vestige]. If Aubrey taps Exotic Orchard, what type(s) of mana can it produce?
entries.reason: The candidate concludes Exotic Orchard produces no mana, but the correct ruling is it can produce any color because Exotic Orchard checks what mana an opponent's land could produce (including one-shot triggered ETB abilities that could add one mana of any color).
entries.answer:
Aubrey's Exotic Orchard produces no mana at all in this situation.

Exotic Orchard says "Add one mana of any color that a land an opponent controls could produce," and Exotic Orchard ruling #3 states plainly that the colors of mana are white, blue, black, red, and green, and that Exotic Orchard can't be tapped for colorless mana even if an opponent's land could produce colorless mana. Nikolas's Crumbling Vestige has only one mana ability while it's on the battlefield: "{T}: Add {C}." {C} is colorless mana specifically, not a color and not generic mana, so it gives Exotic Orchard nothing to copy. With no color available, activating Exotic Orchard's ability produces nothing (compare Exotic Orchard ruling #4, where lands with nothing to point at simply produce no mana).

About Crumbling Vestige's other line, "When this land enters, add one mana of any color": that's a one-shot triggered ability that happened as Crumbling Vestige entered the battlefield and is no longer available. It isn't a mana-producing ability Crumbling Vestige has going forward, so it doesn't turn Exotic Orchard on. (If it had still been a standing ability, Exotic Orchard ruling #0's principle of looking only at what the ability produces, not its cost, would matter — but there's no such ability here to check.)

Two-player vs. multiplayer: Exotic Orchard cares about lands *any* opponent controls, so at a larger table Aubrey should check every opponent's lands, not just Nikolas's. If some other opponent controls a land that could produce a color, Exotic Orchard could be tapped for that color. Assuming Aubrey's only opponent is Nikolas, and Crumbling Vestige is his only land, Exotic Orchard makes nothing.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Any color. Exotic Orchard checks to see what mana Crumbling Vestige could produce if any of its abilities were to resolve at that time. That includes triggered abilities.

entries.question: Azariah, Beckham, and Caelan are playing a multiplayer game. Beckham controls [Stalking Leonin]. Azariah casts [Worst Fears] to take control of Beckham's next turn. After Beckham begins their turn, can Azariah see which player was chosen for the Stalking Leonin?
entries.reason: The candidate reaches the opposite conclusion—the reference says the chosen opponent is not visible to Azariah unless the Leonin's ability is activated, while the candidate asserts Azariah can view the secret choice.
entries.answer:
Yes — while Azariah controls Beckham's turn, Azariah gets to see Beckham's hidden information, which includes the record of the opponent secretly chosen for Stalking Leonin.

Why: Worst Fears says "You see all cards that player could see and make all decisions for them." While controlling Beckham, Azariah sees all cards in the game that Beckham can see, including Beckham's hand and face-down cards Beckham controls [Worst Fears ruling #11], and Azariah makes all choices and decisions Beckham would make, including whether to activate abilities [Worst Fears ruling #1]. Stalking Leonin's secret choice is recorded and kept with the permanent (for example, a slip of paper with the player's name) [Stalking Leonin ruling #2], and it is information Beckham has; since Azariah must decide whether to pay the "Reveal the player you chose" cost and activate Stalking Leonin's ability, Azariah necessarily has access to that recorded choice.

Important limits:
- Azariah controls only the player, not Beckham's permanents — Stalking Leonin stays under Beckham's control [Worst Fears ruling #4]. So if Azariah activates it during that turn, it can only exile a creature attacking Beckham (the ability's controller), and only if that creature is controlled by the opponent Beckham secretly chose. A creature attacking a planeswalker rather than Beckham can't be targeted [Stalking Leonin ruling #4].
- Azariah must use Beckham's resources to pay Beckham's costs, not their own [Worst Fears ruling #8], and can't make illegal choices [Worst Fears ruling #2].
- The chosen player was locked in when Stalking Leonin entered the battlefield; Azariah can't change it. If Beckham never made a choice (e.g., the permanent became a copy of Stalking Leonin), the cost can't be paid at all [Stalking Leonin ruling #0].

Multiplayer note: this is inherently a multiplayer situation (Stalking Leonin requires choosing an opponent, and here there are three players — Azariah, Beckham, and Caelan). Nothing changes about the visibility answer based on player count; the secret choice could be Azariah or Caelan, and Azariah learning it is exactly one of the effects of controlling Beckham.

Timing assumption: I'm assuming Worst Fears already resolved and Beckham's controlled turn has begun, as stated. Before that turn begins, Azariah has no access to the information.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: No. The choice was made as Stalking Leonin entered the battlefield, which already happened- it's no longer visible to Beckham. Azariah can choose to activate the ability (at which point all players will know who was chosen), but otherwise the choice is not visible to any player.

entries.question: Angela controls [Mirror Gallery] and two [Sakashima the Impostor]s. One is a copy of their [Master of the Hunt]; the other is copying a wolf token created by Master of the Hunt. They attack with all four creatures. What are the possible bands that Angela may declare?
entries.reason: The candidate reaches the same conclusion that no bands can be declared because only the token is actually named Wolves of the Hunt and the Sakashimas are still named Sakashima the Impostor, so there are not two creatures with that name to form a band.
entries.answer:
Angela can't declare any bands — all four creatures must attack individually.

The only banding ability in play is the one granted by Master of the Hunt to its tokens: "bands with other creatures named Wolves of the Hunt." As the reminder text on Master of the Hunt spells out, "Any creatures named Wolves of the Hunt can attack in a band as long as at least one has 'bands with other creatures named Wolves of the Hunt.'" That restricts the band to creatures actually named Wolves of the Hunt, and a band needs at least two creatures.

Look at the four attackers:
- Master of the Hunt itself — named Master of the Hunt, has no banding ability, so it can't join.
- The Wolves of the Hunt token — has the banding ability, but it's the only creature with that name on the battlefield.
- The Sakashima the Impostor copying Master of the Hunt — Sakashima the Impostor's own text says the copy's name is Sakashima the Impostor, so it isn't named Wolves of the Hunt (and Master of the Hunt has no banding ability anyway).
- The Sakashima the Impostor copying the Wolves of the Hunt token — it does copy the ability "bands with other creatures named Wolves of the Hunt," but again its name is Sakashima the Impostor, not Wolves of the Hunt, so it isn't a legal member of that band either.

So there's exactly one creature named Wolves of the Hunt, and a one-creature "band" is just a normal attacker. Mirror Gallery is doing real work here (it lets the two legendary Sakashima the Impostors coexist, per Mirror Gallery ruling #0), but it doesn't change any names, so it doesn't enable a band.

If Angela activates Master of the Hunt (or the Sakashima the Impostor that copies Master of the Hunt) before attackers are declared to make a second Wolves of the Hunt token, those two tokens could then attack as a band.

Note: the numbered banding rules weren't provided in my context, so this answer rests on the reminder text printed on Master of the Hunt and on Sakashima the Impostor's name-changing clause; the general banding rules could add further restrictions on band size or composition. Nothing here depends on the number of opponents, though with more than two players every creature in a band would have to be attacking the same defending player or their planeswalker/battle.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: No bands can be declared. The only creature on the battlefield named "Wolves of the Hunt" is the token, so it cannot declare itself as in a band with anything else. The Sakashima the Impostor with "bands with other creatures named Wolves of the Hunt" is not itself named "Wolves of the Hunt", so it cannot declare itself as in a band with the token.

entries.question: Avery controls a Germ token that's equipped with [Barbed Bloodletter]. Nadia controls two [Teferi's Curse]s, one on the Germ, the other on the Barbed Bloodletter. During Avery's untap step, which permanents will phase out? Which of these will phase back in?
entries.reason: The candidate only says the Germ and Bloodletter phase out/in and declines to say whether the two Teferi's Curses (and the token's continued existence) do, whereas the reference states all four permanents phase out and then phase back in.
entries.answer:
Both permanents that Nadia has enchanted — Avery's Germ token and the Barbed Bloodletter equipping it — phase out during Avery's untap step, and both are set to phase back in at the start of Avery's next untap step (before Avery untaps).

Why: "Phasing" means a permanent alternately phases out and phases in; while phased out it's treated as though it doesn't exist. Teferi's Curse grants "Enchanted permanent has phasing," and its reminder text specifies the timing: "It phases in or out before its controller untaps during each of their untap steps." Note that the relevant controller is the controller of the permanent that has phasing (Avery), not Nadia who controls the Auras. So:
- Germ token: has phasing from one Teferi's Curse, is controlled by Avery, so it phases out in Avery's untap step and would phase in during Avery's following untap step.
- Barbed Bloodletter: has phasing from the other Teferi's Curse, is also controlled by Avery, so it likewise phases out now and would phase in during Avery's following untap step.

Two things the provided context does not settle, so I won't guess at them: (1) whether the two Teferi's Curses themselves phase out along with the permanents they enchant (the general phasing rules about attached permanents phasing indirectly weren't provided), and (2) whether a phased-out token like the Germ still exists to phase back in. Those depend on the full phasing rules (and token-existence rules), which aren't in the context here.

Nothing in this interaction depends on the number of players, so the answer is the same in a two-player game or at a multiplayer table.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: All 4 permanents will phase out and phase back in in Ari's next untap step. Barbed Bloodletter and both Teferi's Curses will still be attached to the permanents they were attached to previously. Phasing doesn't cause tokens to cease to exist or unattach permanents from other permanents.

entries.question: Alessandra controls [Sheoldred, the Apocalypse]. During their main phase, they cast [Day's Undoing]. How much life does each player gain/lose?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude that although Sheoldred's abilities trigger from the draws, Day's Undoing ends the turn before those triggers are put on the stack, so none resolve and no life changes occur.
entries.answer:
No life is gained or lost at all.

Day's Undoing makes each player shuffle hand and graveyard into their library and draw seven cards, and Sheoldred, the Apocalypse does trigger — seven times for Alessandra's own draws ("you gain 2 life") and seven times for each opponent's draws ("they lose 2 life"). But because Alessandra cast Day's Undoing on their own turn, Day's Undoing then ends the turn. Per [Day's Undoing ruling #5], any abilities that trigger while players are shuffling cards into their library or drawing seven cards cease to exist when the turn ends — they are never put onto the stack. So all fourteen-plus Sheoldred, the Apocalypse triggers simply vanish and nothing resolves.

Supporting detail: ending the turn exiles everything on the stack, and during that process no player gets priority and no triggered abilities are put onto the stack ([Day's Undoing ruling #4]). The only triggers that could still matter are ones put onto the stack during the cleanup step ([Day's Undoing ruling #2]), which is not the case for these draw triggers.

Two players vs. multiplayer: the result is the same. With more opponents there are simply more Sheoldred, the Apocalypse triggers for the extra players' draws, and all of them equally cease to exist, so no player at the table loses or gains life.

Timing caveat: this assumes Day's Undoing resolved on Alessandra's own turn, as stated. If Day's Undoing had somehow resolved during another player's turn, the turn would not end, and then all the Sheoldred, the Apocalypse triggers would resolve normally — Alessandra would gain 14 life, and each opponent would lose 14 life (with Alessandra choosing the order of simultaneous-draw triggers, per [Sheoldred, the Apocalypse ruling #0]).

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: None. The players first draw seven cards each, triggering Sheoldred, the Apocalypse fourteen times. Then Alessandra ends the turn, which nullifies those triggers before they're even put onto the stack.

entries.question: It is currently day and Adonis controls [Lazotep Convert] (the back face of [Invasion of Amonkhet]), which is a copy of [Kessig Naturalist]. What happens if it becomes night?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude Lazotep Convert remains a copy of Kessig Naturalist and will not transform at night because the back face is already up and there is no applicable night face for it to become.
entries.answer:
Nothing changes about Adonis's permanent: Lazotep Convert copying Kessig Naturalist does not transform when it becomes night. It stays on the battlefield as a 2/2 Human Werewolf named Kessig Naturalist (a 4/4 black Zombie in addition to its other colors and types, per Lazotep Convert's own text), keeping daybound.

Why: Lazotep Convert's copy effect copies exactly what was printed on the copied creature card [Invasion of Amonkhet // Lazotep Convert ruling #12], so it gains Kessig Naturalist's printed text, including daybound. Normally daybound permanents transform to their nightbound faces as it becomes night, immediately and not as a state-based action [Kessig Naturalist // Lord of the Ulvenwald ruling #2]. But the physical card here is Invasion of Amonkhet // Lazotep Convert, already on its Lazotep Convert (back) face; the copy effect only gives it the copiable characteristics of the Kessig Naturalist face, not Lord of the Ulvenwald as a second face to turn to. With no Lord of the Ulvenwald face available to it, the daybound transform simply can't happen and the permanent is unaffected. Note also that permanents with daybound/nightbound can't transform by any other means [Kessig Naturalist // Lord of the Ulvenwald ruling #8], so no other effect will flip it back to Invasion of Amonkhet either.

Timing note: I'm assuming Lazotep Convert was already on the battlefield as a copy of Kessig Naturalist before night fell. If instead it were entering the battlefield while it is already night, the daybound rule about entering with the nightbound face up [Kessig Naturalist // Lord of the Ulvenwald ruling #6] still couldn't apply, for the same reason — there is no Lord of the Ulvenwald face for it, so it just enters as the Kessig Naturalist copy.

Caveat: the provided context doesn't include the general copy rules (what a copy of a double-faced card copies), so that step of the reasoning rests on Lazotep Convert ruling #12 rather than a quoted numbered rule. Day/night is a game-wide designation, so this works the same in two-player and multiplayer games [Kessig Naturalist // Lord of the Ulvenwald ruling #4].

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Lazotep Convert will be a copy of Kessig Naturalist. As it becomes night, it will not transform and remain a copy of Kessig Naturalist. Lazotep Convert will only copy the front face of Kessig Naturalist and does not copy its status. When it becomes night, it will not transform because a daybound permanent will only transform as it becomes night if it is front face up. ([702.145b])

entries.question: Adelina's [Fireblade Charger] dies, and Nasir responds with [Thwart the Enemy]. Is the damage prevented?
entries.reason: The candidate gives a definitive "no" ruling, whereas the reference says the interaction is unclear/ambiguous and not definitively settled.
entries.answer:
No — Thwart the Enemy does not prevent Fireblade Charger's death-trigger damage.

Why: Thwart the Enemy only prevents damage "that would be dealt this turn by creatures your opponents control." Once Fireblade Charger has died, it is a card in Adelina's graveyard, not a creature Adelina controls on the battlefield, so the damage source isn't among the objects Thwart the Enemy covers. Fireblade Charger's triggered ability ("When this creature dies, it deals damage equal to its power to any target") still resolves, using Fireblade Charger's last known existence on the battlefield to determine its power — if that power was 0 or less, the ability simply does nothing [Fireblade Charger ruling #0].

Timing assumption: I'm assuming Nasir cast Thwart the Enemy in response to the death trigger (i.e., after Fireblade Charger had already left the battlefield). That's the only order the question describes. If instead Thwart the Enemy had resolved earlier in the turn while Fireblade Charger was still on the battlefield, the answer would be the same for the death trigger, because at the time that damage is actually dealt Fireblade Charger is no longer a creature an opponent controls — the prevention effect's description of the source is checked when the damage would be dealt.

Multiplayer note: nothing here changes with more than two players. Thwart the Enemy says "creatures your opponents control," so it would cover on-battlefield creatures of every opponent, not just Adelina's — but Fireblade Charger in the graveyard is still not covered.

Practical upshot: Nasir needs a way to prevent or redirect damage from a non-creature/graveyard source, or to reduce Fireblade Charger's power before it dies, rather than Thwart the Enemy.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Unclear. Fireblade Charger is not currently a creature on the battlefield, but the game uses its last known information to determine how the damage is dealt. If Fireblade Charger only applies to objects that are creatures, like how Biomantic Mastery only counts creatures that actually exist on the battlefield, it won't be prevented. But if Fireblade Charger checks the source of damage to see whether it's a creature, it will be able to identify the damage as coming from a creature. The intention is probably the latter, but Wizards has not clarified.

2) What the Copy Artifact was. If instead no such trigger happened, Viashino Warrior was never on the battlefield at all and the only result of the last activation is that the Copy Artifact becomes a 6/4 Streetbreaker Wurm copy.

entries.question: Adelyn controls [Panharmonicon] and [Mycosynth Lattice] and has [Dwarven Trader] and [Staunch Shieldmate] in their graveyard. They cast [Animate Dead] targeting Dwarven Trader. What happens as it enters the battlefield?

entries.question: Avery controls [Caelorna, Coral Tyrant] and [Darksteel Garrison] that's fortifying [Spire Garden]. Avery casts [Bludgeon Brawl]. entries.question: Abel attacks with [Pristine Angel]. While it's tapped, Nico activates [Cephalid Snitch]'s ability targeting Pristine Angel. After that resolves, Abel casts a spell and untaps Pristine Angel. Can Nico now target the Pristine Angel with [Murder]?

Paying Boris Devilboon's cost: the cost is {2}{B}{R} plus tapping Boris Devilboon. The {C}{C} from Krark-Clan Ironworks can pay the {2} generic portion directly; alternatively, Mycosynth Lattice's third ability ("Players may spend mana as though it were mana of any color") lets that colorless mana pay the {B} and {R}, since Krark-Clan Ironworks' mana carries no restriction on what it can be spent on [Mycosynth Lattice ruling #0]. Either way the cost is payable, with the remaining symbols covered by Alex's other mana.

Who controls the ability: Alex. Alex was the controller of Boris Devilboon (via Control Magic's "You control enchanted creature") at the time the ability was activated, and the ability on the stack is a separate object from Boris Devilboon — losing control of Boris Devilboon mid-activation doesn't change who controls the already-activated ability. So Alex creates the 1/1 black and red Minor Demon token (which Mycosynth Lattice's second ability will make colorless — everything in every zone is colorless [Mycosynth Lattice ruling #2] — and Mycosynth Lattice's first ability will also make it an artifact).

Side effect: once Control Magic leaves the battlefield as a cost, its control effect ends and Boris Devilboon reverts to Nico's control, tapped. Note that Boris Devilboon must already have been under Alex's control long enough to use its {T} ability (no haste granted here) — I'm assuming that's the case.

Caveat on grounding: the numbered rules provided here don't include the rules on paying activation costs or on an ability existing independently of its source, so that part of the answer rests on the card texts and rulings above. Nothing in this interaction changes between a two-player game and a multiplayer table.

Yes, this is legal, and Alex will control the ability. The process for activating an ability is the same as the process for casting a spell. The first step of activating an ability is to put it onto the stack. Mana abilities are activated in a later step. The ability is already on the stack at this point (controlled by Alex), so the Boris Devilboon changing controllers won't change who controls the ability. After activating mana abilities, Alex must pay the activation cost. {T} means "tap this permanent", so Alex can pay the cost regardless of who controls the Boris Devilboon at that time.

Legality is checked before mana abilities are activated, so it won't matter that Boris Devilboon gets summoning sickness when it changes controllers.

entries.question: Nico has cast a [Gather Specimens] earlier in the turn. Aiden controls a [Chronatog Totem] that is currently a creature due to its own ability, and casts an [Evil Twin], choosing to have it copy Chronatog Totem. What happens?
entries.reason: Both state Gather Specimens causes Evil Twin to enter under Nico's control and that Nico, not Aiden, chooses what it copies.
entries.answer:
Short answer: Nico's Gather Specimens applies, so the Evil Twin permanent enters the battlefield under Nico's control — and because the copy choice is a "as it enters" choice, it's Nico, not Aiden, who chooses what Evil Twin copies. If Nico chooses Chronatog Totem, Evil Twin enters as a copy of Chronatog Totem's printed characteristics: a noncreature artifact (not a creature), so it does not die as a 0/0, and it has the extra ability "{U}{B}, {T}: Destroy target creature with the same name as this creature."

Details:

1) Gather Specimens says "If a creature would enter the battlefield under an opponent's control this turn, it enters under your control instead." Evil Twin is a creature spell that would resolve and enter as a creature under Aiden's control, so Gather Specimens replaces that and it enters under Nico's control. Choices Aiden made while casting are remembered [Gather Specimens ruling #6], and Gather Specimens is not targeted and applies to any opponent's creature [Gather Specimens ruling #4].

2) Gather Specimens' replacement effect is applied before other effects that modify how the permanent enters, including copy choices — the cited example is exactly Clone: "If Clone would enter under an opponent's control, you choose which creature it copies as it enters under your control" [Gather Specimens ruling #3]. So Aiden doesn't get to lock in the copy choice; Nico makes it. Nico may pick any creature on the battlefield, or pick nothing (in which case Evil Twin is a 0/0 and dies) [Evil Twin ruling #4].

3) If Nico picks Chronatog Totem: Evil Twin copies only what is printed on Chronatog Totem, not the temporary effect from Chronatog Totem's "{1}{U}: This artifact becomes a 1/2 blue Atog artifact creature until end of turn" — copy effects don't copy non-copy effects that changed types or power/toughness [Evil Twin ruling #7]. So Nico's permanent is a plain Chronatog Totem artifact (no power/toughness at all, hence no 0/0 death), with the mana ability, the animation ability, the +3/+3/skip-a-turn ability, and the gained "{U}{B}, {T}: Destroy target creature with the same name as this creature" ability [Evil Twin ruling #0].

4) Using that destroy ability against Aiden's Chronatog Totem requires a legal target — a creature named Chronatog Totem — so Aiden's must still be animated. Also, Nico's new permanent can't use {T} abilities (including the destroy ability and the mana ability) this turn: a permanent's {T} abilities can be activated only if its controller has continuously controlled it since the beginning of their most recent turn, regardless of how long it's been a creature [Chronatog Totem ruling #0]. Any "enters" triggers of the copied card would trigger normally [Evil Twin ruling #6].

Timing note: I'm assuming Gather Specimens resolved before Evil Twin resolves, as stated. Gather Specimens does not retroactively change control of creatures that already entered this turn [Gather Specimens ruling #0], so it has no effect on Aiden's already-on-the-battlefield Chronatog Totem.

Multiplayer: Gather Specimens applies to creatures entering under any opponent's control, so at a larger table every opponent's entering creatures are affected, not just Aiden's [Gather Specimens ruling #4]. If another player also cast Gather Specimens this turn, the would-be controller chooses which one applies first, and the process repeats [Gather Specimens ruling #5], which with exactly two opposing Gather Specimens results in the creature entering under the first player's control [Gather Specimens ruling #8].

entries.question: Albert and Nico are beginning the game and have just drawn 7 cards. Albert has [Serum Powder] in their hand. Does Albert get to know whether Nico is going to mulligan before deciding whether to use Serum Powder's ability?
entries.reason: The candidate says the order is unsettled and declines to conclude whether Albert sees Nico's mulligan choice, whereas the reference gives a definitive "No" that Albert does not get to know Nico's decision.
entries.answer:
The provided rules don't settle this. Answering it requires the opening-hand/mulligan procedure rule (the rule that governs how and in what order each player declares whether they will mulligan), and that rule is not in the context given to me.

What the context does tell you: Serum Powder's ability may be used "any time you could mulligan and this card is in your hand," and using it doesn't stop Albert from taking further mulligans afterward, nor does taking a mulligan stop Albert from using a Serum Powder drawn in the new hand [Serum Powder ruling #1]. Cards Albert exiles this way stay exiled for the whole game and are not shuffled back on a later mulligan [Serum Powder ruling #0]. So Albert's decision is not one-shot — Albert can still mulligan after exiling, or exile after mulliganing.

The only ordering rule available is the general APNAP rule: when multiple players would make choices at the same time, the active player chooses first, then the other players in turn order, and a player knows the choices made by the previous players when making their own [101.4b]. That is a general rule for simultaneous choices, not specifically the mulligan step, so I can't use it to state whether Albert sees Nico's mulligan declaration first. Note also that whether Albert or Nico chooses first would depend on who is the active (starting) player, which the question doesn't say.

This reasoning is framed for the two-player game Albert and Nico are playing; the context contains no multiplayer-specific mulligan rules, so a larger table may resolve declaration order differently.

entries.answer_gold: No. Albert exiles their hand and draws 7 cards at the time they would normally declare if they are going to take a mulligan, which is before Nico has made that decision.

entries.question: Ariana controls [Sen Triplets], which targeted Nico. Nico's hand contains [Rift Sower]. Can either player suspend it? If so, who will cast it once the last time counter is removed?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude that neither player can suspend Rift Sower while Sen Triplets' restriction applies and that only the card's owner (Nico) can suspend it later and cast it when the last counter is removed.
entries.answer:
Direct answer: Ariana cannot suspend Rift Sower, and during the turn Sen Triplets' ability is active Nico can't either; on a later turn (typically Nico's own main phase) Nico can suspend it, and Nico is the player who gets the option to cast it when the last time counter is removed.

Why Ariana can't: Sen Triplets only grants "You may play lands and cast spells from that player's hand this turn." Exiling a card with suspend is not casting it and doesn't use the stack [Rift Sower ruling #4], so that permission doesn't cover it. And Sen Triplets doesn't let Ariana activate abilities of cards in Nico's hand [Sen Triplets ruling #0]. Suspend's first component is a static ability that lets the card's own controller exile it from their hand [Rift Sower ruling #8] — it isn't something Ariana is given access to.

Why Nico can't during that turn: you may exile a card with suspend only at a time you could cast that card, taking into account effects that stop you from casting it [Rift Sower ruling #0]. Sen Triplets says Nico "can't cast spells or activate abilities" this turn, so there is no legal window for Nico to suspend Rift Sower during that turn. (Note Sen Triplets' restriction is broader than just abilities — it also blocks mana abilities [Sen Triplets ruling #5] — but the barrier to suspending here is the can't-cast clause, since suspend timing is keyed to casting timing.) In practice this rarely matters: Sen Triplets triggers at Ariana's upkeep and lasts only that turn, while Rift Sower is a creature card castable only in Nico's own main phase — a turn on which the restriction isn't in effect.

Once suspended, the card is exiled face up with time counters [Rift Sower ruling #10]. The suspend triggered abilities belong to Nico as the suspending player: at the beginning of Nico's upkeep a counter is removed, and when the last is removed the third suspend ability triggers and Nico may cast it [Rift Sower ruling #8], [Rift Sower ruling #3]. Nico isn't required to cast it [Rift Sower ruling #5]. Ariana never gets to cast it, because Sen Triplets only lets Ariana cast spells from Nico's hand — the exile zone is a different zone.

Timing assumption: I'm assuming Sen Triplets' upkeep trigger has already resolved naming Nico when the suspend attempt happens. If instead Nico suspends Rift Sower before that trigger resolves (or on a turn Nico isn't the chosen opponent), suspending is legal with no restriction at all.

Multiplayer: this works the same with two players or more. Sen Triplets targets one chosen opponent each upkeep, so only that one player is restricted; other opponents are unaffected and could suspend their own cards freely.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Neither player can suspend it. Only a card's owner has the option to suspend it, and only if they have permission to cast it.

entries.question: Ariella controls a manifested [Wayward Angel] and has 7 cards in their graveyard. Nathaniel casts [Turn to Frog], targeting Wayward Angel. After that resolves, Ariella turns Wayward Angel face up. What are Wayward Angel's characteristics afterwards?
entries.reason: The candidate concludes the Angel becomes a 1/1 blue Frog with no abilities, whereas the reference states it ends up a 4/4 black Frog with trample and the upkeep-sacrifice ability, so the rulings conflict.
entries.answer:
Wayward Angel ends up as a 1/1 blue Frog creature named Wayward Angel with no abilities (its mana cost is still {4}{W}{W}, so its mana value is 6; it retains any supertypes it had, of which it has none).

Why: Turn to Frog's effect ("Until end of turn, target creature loses all abilities and becomes a blue Frog with base power and toughness 1/1") keeps applying to that permanent for the rest of the turn, even after Ariella takes the special action of turning it face up. Turning face up changes what the object's printed/base characteristics are, but Turn to Frog is still layered on top of whatever those characteristics are — the same way a Theros God turned to a Frog still ends up a 1/1 blue Frog with no abilities even though its own type-changing ability would otherwise apply [Turn to Frog ruling #4].

So after it's turned face up:
- Colors: blue only — not white, and not black, because the Threshold ability that would have made it black is removed [Turn to Frog ruling #1], [Wayward Angel ruling #0].
- Types: creature — Frog only; Angel and Horror are gone [Turn to Frog ruling #1].
- Abilities: none. Flying, vigilance, and the Threshold ability (+3/+3, black, trample, "At the beginning of your upkeep, sacrifice a creature") are all stripped, so the seven cards in Ariella's graveyard do nothing here. Note that Turn to Frog only removes abilities; it doesn't retroactively remove abilities that already triggered [Turn to Frog ruling #5], and any ability granted to it after Turn to Frog resolved by some other effect would stick [Turn to Frog ruling #3] — turning face up is not such a grant.
- Power/toughness: base 1/1, plus any P/T-modifying effects or counters, which still apply regardless of timestamp [Turn to Frog ruling #2].

Timing note: I'm assuming the order you gave — Turn to Frog resolves first, then Wayward Angel is turned face up. If instead Ariella had turned it face up first and Turn to Frog resolved afterward, the end result this turn would be the same: a 1/1 blue Frog with no abilities.

Caveat: the rules excerpts provided don't include the manifest rules or the layer (dependency/timestamp) rules, so the reasoning above leans on the Turn to Frog and Wayward Angel rulings supplied. Nothing here depends on player count, so the answer is the same in a two-player game or at a multiplayer table.

entries.answer_gold: It's a 4/4 black Frog with trample and "At the beginning of your upkeep, sacrifice a creature", but no other abilities. Wayward Angel receives a new timestamp when it turns face up, so its ability is applied before Turn to Frog in each layer. Wayward Angel's last ability is removed by Turn to Frog in layer 6, but since it's already started to apply in layer 5 to change its color to black, it will continue doing so in later layers. Turn to Frog has the earlier timestamp, so it makes Wayward Angel blue before it becomes black in layer 5 and removes Wayward Angel's abilities in layer 6 before it gains trample and "At the beginning of your upkeep, sacrifice a creature".

entries.question: Ahmad controls [Conspiracy] (naming "Ferret"), [Kormus Bell], [Urborg, Tomb of Yawgmoth], and a [Vastwood Zendikon] enchanting Urborg, Tomb of Yawgmoth that entered the battlefield in that order. Is Urborg, Tomb of Yawgmoth a creature? If so, what are its creature types?
entries.reason: The candidate concludes Urborg is only a Ferret (Conspiracy removing Elemental), while the reference says it is Elemental Ferret (Vastwood Zendikon's Elemental type remains), so the final creature-type rulings conflict.
entries.answer:
Yes — Urborg, Tomb of Yawgmoth is a creature (and still a land), and its only creature type is Ferret.

Why it's a creature: Urborg, Tomb of Yawgmoth's own text makes each land a Swamp in addition to its other land types, and that includes Urborg, Tomb of Yawgmoth itself while it's on the battlefield [Urborg, Tomb of Yawgmoth ruling #0, Urborg, Tomb of Yawgmoth ruling #2]. Kormus Bell then makes all Swamps 1/1 black creatures that are still lands, and it applies to Swamps controlled by any player [Kormus Bell ruling #1, Kormus Bell ruling #0]. On top of that, Vastwood Zendikon makes the enchanted land a 6/4 green Elemental creature that's still a land, and its power/toughness setting overwrites the earlier 1/1 from Kormus Bell because it has the later timestamp [Vastwood Zendikon ruling #0, Vastwood Zendikon ruling #5]. So Urborg, Tomb of Yawgmoth is a 6/4 land creature.

Why the type is just Ferret: Conspiracy says creatures you control are the chosen type, and affected creatures lose all of their other creature types [Conspiracy ruling #4]. Conspiracy also explicitly can grant a creature type to animated lands that would otherwise have none [Conspiracy ruling #1]. Since Ahmad controls this land creature, Conspiracy overwrites Elemental (from Vastwood Zendikon) and any type from Kormus Bell, leaving Ferret alone. Note that Swamp is a land type, not a creature type, so Urborg, Tomb of Yawgmoth remains a Swamp land as well — Conspiracy only touches creature types.

One transparency note: the full layer/timestamp/dependency rules that formally put Conspiracy's effect after Vastwood Zendikon's "Elemental" weren't included in the context provided to me (only the control-changing layer, rule 613.1b, was). The result above follows from Conspiracy's own ruling that affected creatures lose all other creature types [Conspiracy ruling #4]. Nothing here depends on the number of players; the answer is the same in a two-player game or at a multiplayer table, since Kormus Bell affects every player's Swamps [Kormus Bell ruling #1].

entries.answer_gold: It is an Elemental Ferret creature. Conspiracy has the earliest timestamp, but it's dependent on Vastwood Zendikon, and waits to apply until after Vastwood Zendikon is applied. Kormus Bell is dependent on Urborg, Tomb of Yawgmoth, so Urborg, Tomb of Yawgmoth is applied first, then Kormus Bell. At this point Conspiracy is no longer be dependent on Vastwood Zendikon, so Conspiracy is applied, and then Vastwood Zendikon. Since Vastwood Zendikon says that Urborg, Tomb of Yawgmoth is still a land, it retains its prior creature type of "Ferret" when it becomes an Elemental.
